world_behind.title: What the request actually cost
world_behind.text: They are the king's sons and the kingdom's heirs. Going up to the land of Nephi means leaving the succession and walking into the country of a people the record has described as hating the Nephites since Lehi's generation. The father does not decide it himself; he goes and inquires of the Lord.

world_behind.title: Where they proposed to go
world_behind.text: The land of Nephi is the country their own people abandoned two generations earlier, where Zeniff's colony was taxed into bondage and Abinadi was burned. The record has spent sixteen chapters establishing what that place does to Nephites, and these four are asking to walk into it.

world_behind.title: Two reasons offered, and neither is ranked
world_behind.text: They could not bear that any human soul should perish; and they were the very vilest of sinners. Compassion and autobiography are set side by side in consecutive verses, and the record does not say which produced the other.

world_behind.title: How long they were gone
world_behind.text: This chapter says only that they took their journey and that an account would follow. From the far end, Ammon reports that they had been teaching among the Lamanites for the space of fourteen years. Four princes leave the country for a decade and a half, and the departure gets one clause.

world_behind.title: What the interpreters were
world_behind.text: Two stones fastened into the two rims of a bow, prepared from the beginning and handed down through generations for interpreting languages. The record describes the object physically, states its purpose, and then names the office attached to it.

world_behind.title: The last chapter dated by a reign
world_behind.text: Everything up to here is counted in kings: the reign of Zeniff, of Noah, of Mosiah. The next chapter installs judges, and from Alma 1:1 onward this record counts its years by the reign of the judges instead. How time is measured changes one chapter after this one.

words.text: To persuade by evidence, in the older sense that carries a hint of proving someone wrong. What they hope to convince the Lamanites of is the iniquity of their fathers. The argument is aimed at a tradition. It is the second item on their list and the hardest.

The most worthless or contemptible. The record applies the superlative to the four princes and Alma's son, in a verse that also says the Spirit worked upon them and the Lord spared them. Nothing softens the word; it stands next to the mercy without qualification.

To bestow formally, the verb this record uses for handing over an office. Treated at Mosiah 1:9. It appears twice in the chapter. The kingdom cannot be conferred at verse 10; the records are conferred at verse 20. One transfer fails and the other succeeds, in the same word.

Restless concern, a pressing want rather than modern nervousness. Treated at 2 Nephi 1:16. It is given as the reason a king spent his time translating: the great anxiety of his people to know what had happened to a destroyed civilization. Public curiosity is treated as sufficient cause.

The outer edges of a circular frame. The verse is unusually concrete about the instrument: two stones fastened into two rims of a bow. The record rarely describes an object this precisely, and it does so here without explaining how the thing works.

Confused, thrown into disorder. Treated at 1 Nephi 14:2. The record says it of a language rather than of people. The chapter reaches back past every event in this record to the moment speech itself divided, which is also the moment the people whose bones were found began.

phrases.term: Cure them of their hatred towards the Nephites
phrases.text: Hatred described as a condition with a possible remedy, and the phrase occurs once in scripture. The verb is medical. Four centuries of enmity are treated here as something a people might recover from.

phrases.term: They could not bear that any human soul should perish
phrases.text: The motive, stated as an inability. What follows in the same verse is physical: the very thought of a soul enduring endless torment made them quake and tremble. The record grounds a decade of missionary work in a reaction of the body.

phrases.term: The Lord saw fit in his infinite mercy to spare them
phrases.text: The same construction the record used of the Lord's decisions about two peoples in bondage. There he did not see fit to deliver one, and saw fit to chasten the other. Here it governs a sparing, and the clause that follows says they still suffered much anguish of soul.

phrases.term: I will deliver thy sons out of the hands of the Lamanites
phrases.text: A promise made to a father rather than to the men going. It is specific, it is conditional on nothing, and the record spends a large part of the next book showing it kept, including the occasions when they were in fact in Lamanite hands.

phrases.term: There was not any of his sons who would accept of the kingdom
phrases.text: The constitutional crisis, reported as a fact about four young men's preferences. Nothing suggests they were disqualified or that anyone objected to them. They simply would not take it, and the verse before has them leaving the country.

phrases.term: Desirous beyond measure to know concerning those people who had been destroyed
phrases.text: The reason given for translating the plates, and it is curiosity. Limhi had said almost the same thing to Ammon twenty chapters earlier (Mosiah 8:12). A whole people wanted to know what had happened, and the king answered by producing a translation.

phrases.term: Whosoever has these things is called seer, after the manner of old times
phrases.text: An office defined by custody of an object. The last clause reaches for a precedent the record does not spell out, and the phrase occurs once in scripture. Ammon had given Limhi a fuller definition; this one is shorter and entirely practical.

phrases.term: Even from that time back until the creation of Adam
phrases.text: The reach of the translated record, given as a single span. It runs from a civilization's destruction back through the confounding of language to the first man. What has just been handed to this people is a history longer than their own by an order of magnitude.

verses.label: v. 6–8
verses.title: He asks permission and receives a forecast
verses.text: Mosiah "inquired of the Lord if he should let his sons go up among the Lamanites to preach the word" — a yes-or-no question. The answer supplies three things nobody asked for: many shall believe, they shall have eternal life, and the sons will be delivered. The record prints the request and the reply close enough together that the reader can see how much the second exceeds the first.

verses.label: v. 11–13
verses.title: A translation undertaken because the public wanted it
verses.text: The reason given is not revelation or command but demand: the great anxiety of his people, who wished to know about the destroyed nation. The method is then described as hardware, two stones fastened into the rims of a bow. Motive is curiosity, means is an instrument, and the record supplies both before it says a word about what the plates contained.

verses.label: v. 20
verses.title: The handover is an inventory and a command to continue
verses.text: The plates of brass, all the things kept, all the records, and the interpreters, conferred on Alma with an instruction to keep, preserve and record, "even as they had been handed down from the time that Lehi left Jerusalem." The charge is stated as continuation of a chain, the same shape Alma will use on his own son at Alma 37:2.

chapter.title: The missionary motive is a reaction the record already catalogued
chapter.text: When both accounts were read aloud in Zarahemla, the fifth thing the assembly felt was pain and anguish for the welfare of Lamanite souls. This chapter opens with four men who cannot bear that any soul should perish. The book turns an emotion recorded three chapters earlier into a journey.

chapter.title: Two causes are given and left unranked
chapter.text: Compassion for souls, and having been the vilest of sinners. The record puts them in consecutive verses without a connective, so the reader can take the second as explaining the first or as merely accompanying it.

chapter.title: The mission is also foreign policy
chapter.text: Cure their hatred, make them friendly, end contentions in the land. Three of the five stated aims are about the relationship between two nations.

chapter.title: A constitutional crisis in one sentence
chapter.text: No one to confer the kingdom upon. Verse 10 does not present itself as important, and the whole of the next chapter exists because of it: judges, law, the voice of the people, the end of the monarchy.

chapter.title: The same verb governs the failure and the success
chapter.text: The kingdom cannot be conferred; the records are conferred. What Mosiah cannot pass to a son he passes to a high priest, and the chapter puts the two transfers ten verses apart.

chapter.title: A book is promised here and delivered much later
chapter.text: "This account shall be written hereafter." The twenty-four plates found by a lost search party, translated by a king, become the Book of Ether near the end of the record, and the promise is made here in passing.

chapter.title: The office is defined by possession
chapter.text: Whosoever has these things is called seer. Ammon's definition to Limhi had been about power and revelation; this one is about who is holding the stones. The record gives both and reconciles neither.

chapter.title: Role in the book
chapter.text: Mosiah 27 converted the sons of Mosiah; this chapter sends them away and empties the throne; Mosiah 29 replaces the monarchy. It also closes the record's own housekeeping. The Jaredite plates are translated and the archive has a new keeper before the government changes.

applications.title: Ask before you go
applications.text: They pleaded with their father for many days, and he inquired of the Lord before answering. Neither the asking nor the checking was treated as a delay; both were part of doing the thing properly.

applications.title: Name the hatred as curable
applications.text: They set out to cure the Lamanites of hatred. Where you are facing long-standing enmity, the word you use for it shapes what you think can be attempted.

applications.title: Let your worst history be part of the reason
applications.text: The record says they were the vilest of sinners in the same breath as it explains why they went. The chapter neither hides that nor dwells on it. It puts the fact next to the motive.

applications.title: Answer curiosity when you can
applications.text: The people were desirous beyond measure to know, so the king translated a record. Wanting to know is treated here as a good enough reason to do a great deal of work.

applications.title: Pass on what you cannot pass down
applications.text: The kingdom had no heir; the records did. When one line of succession closes, look at what else you are holding that still needs a keeper.

applications.title: Write it so somebody can have it later
applications.text: The charge is to keep, preserve, record, and hand down. Three of those four verbs are about the future.

applications.title: Put your own account in proportion
applications.text: They learned they were recent. A record reaching back to the creation put their own account in proportion, and the response was both mourning and rejoicing.

questions.text: What enmity in my life have I stopped treating as curable?
Whose perishing would I actually find unbearable?
What part of my own history belongs in my reasons rather than in my apologies?
What am I holding that nobody has agreed to take from me?
What do I want to know badly enough to do the work?
What am I keeping that is meant for someone I will not meet?
